newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers delay decision on beef labels.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers delay decision on beef labels.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Monday postponed a decision on a compromise on compulsory beef labelling after unanimously rejecting a proposal that would give the European Parliament a joint say, Dutch officials said.
The compromise, drafted by the Dutch EU Presidency, would give the parliament only a consultative role, but would still make it obligatory to state the origin of beef sold in shops from January 2000.
"We are breaking off early tonight because we're planning on a late night session tomorrow," a Dutch official said.

Farm ministers are facing increased pressure to improve food safety after a European Commission report last week revealed widespread failures among EU countries to detect and eradicate the fatal brain wasting disease known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).

The Commission recently revised a proposal on identification of cattle and beef labelling, aimed at restoring consumer confidence after the mad cow disease health scare, to take account of European Parliament demands.
"No one supported the European Commission," a Commission spokesman said, referring to greater parliamentary powers.
Italy, noting virtual agreement on identification but divisions over labelling, wanted to split the proposal but this was opposed by the Commission.
Cattle would be identified by eartags, passports and registered on computerised data bases from January 2000.
A majority, led by France and Germany, were in favour of compulsory beef labelling but others, notably Britain, Ireland and Italy had strong objections.
"I am in favour, very much in favour and even more so in favour," French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur told Reuters before the meeting, adding he hoped that agreement would rapidly be reached.

Portuguese Farm Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva, another supporter of compulsory labelling, said the proposal must be changed but it would need unanimous agreement among the 15 member states to overrule the Commission.
Danish Farm Minister Henrik Dam Kristensen said he did not think agreement would be reached.
"I'm a little bit pessimistic," he told reporters before the meeting. "I think the proposal is too bureaucratic."
British officials said Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg would ask for more time to study the revised proposal, presented earlier this month, as there were points he didn't like.
Britain believes that the proposal would stir nationalist sentiment and create a barrier to trade in the EU single market.
